items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the actual rate at which temperature falls with height in the atmosphere at a given time and place, on average about 6.5 °C per 1000 m”.
items.answer: Environmental lapse rate (ELR)
items.markingKey: Environmental lapse rate (ELR): the actual rate at which temperature falls with height in the atmosphere at a given time and place, on average about 6.5 °C per 1000 m. [1]

items.stem: Explain why rising air cools.
items.answer: Pressure falls with height, so rising air expands; expansion uses energy, so the air cools adiabatically (without heat exchange with its surroundings).
items.markingKey: 1 mark expansion; 1 mark energy/adiabatic [2]

items.stem: Explain conditional instability.
items.answer: The ELR lies between the SALR and DALR; unsaturated rising air cools at the DALR and is cooler than its surroundings (stable); once condensation occurs it cools at the slower SALR and may become warmer than the surroundings, so it continues to rise (unstable).
items.markingKey: 1 mark definition; 1 mark below condensation; 1 mark above [3]

items.stem: Air at sea level with a temperature of 28 °C and a dew point of 18 °C is forced to rise over a mountain range 3 000 m high, then descends to sea level on the other side. Assume a DALR of 10 °C per 1000 m, a SALR of 7 °C per 1000 m, that condensation begins when the air has cooled to 18 °C, and that all moisture is lost as precipitation on the windward side. Calculate the height of the condensation level.

Air at sea level with a temperature of 19 °C and a dew point of 12 °C is forced to rise over a mountain range 3 500 m high, then descends to sea level on the other side. Assume a DALR of 10 °C per 1000 m, a SALR of 5 °C per 1000 m, that condensation begins when the air has cooled to 12 °C, and that all moisture is lost as precipitation on the windward side. (a) Calculate the temperature of the air at the summit. (b) Calculate the temperature of the air when it reaches sea level on the leeward side.
items.markingKey: (a) 19 − 10 × 0.7 = 12 °C at condensation level; then − 5 × 2.8 = -2 °C [2] (b) descends dry at the DALR: -2 + 10 × 3.5 = 33 °C [2]

items.stem: Air at sea level with a temperature of 19 °C and a dew point of 11 °C is forced to rise over a mountain range 3 500 m high, then descends to sea level on the other side. Assume a DALR of 10 °C per 1000 m, a SALR of 6 °C per 1000 m, that condensation begins when the air has cooled to 11 °C, and that all moisture is lost as precipitation on the windward side. (a) Calculate the temperature of the air when it reaches sea level on the leeward side. (b) On another day the ELR is 4 °C per 1000 m. State the stability of the atmosphere and give a reason.
items.answer: (a) 29.8 °C (b) Absolutely stable: the ELR is less than the SALR, so rising air is always cooler than its surroundings.
items.markingKey: (a) descends dry at the DALR: -5.2 + 10 × 3.5 = 29.8 °C [2] (b) 1 mark state; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that atmospheric stability is the most important factor in determining the type of precipitation an area receives.
items.answer: For: Unstable air produces convective showers, thunderstorms and hail; stable air gives drizzle, fog and dry weather. Against: Temperature (rain, snow or hail), moisture supply, uplift mechanisms (relief, fronts, convergence), condensation nuclei and cloud processes also matter. Conclusion: Stability controls whether air rises far enough to give heavy precipitation, but moisture and temperature control the amount and form.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “environmental lapse rate (ELR)”?
options: When the ELR is less than the SALR, so a rising parcel is always cooler than its surroundings and sinks back.
The rate at which saturated rising air cools, about 4-9 °C per 1000 m, slower because latent heat is released by condensation.
The actual rate at which temperature falls with height in the atmosphere at a given time and place, on average about 6.5 °C per 1000 m.
The rate at which unsaturated rising air cools by expansion, about 10 °C per 1000 m.
items.answer: The actual rate at which temperature falls with height in the atmosphere at a given time and place, on average about 6.5 °C per 1000 m.
items.markingKey: Environmental lapse rate (ELR): the actual rate at which temperature falls with height in the atmosphere at a given time and place, on average about 6.5 °C per 1000 m. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “The DALR changes from day to day.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. The DALR is fixed (about 10 °C/km); it is the ELR that varies.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain how relative humidity changes during a clear day if absolute humidity stays constant.
items.answer: As temperature rises the air can hold more vapour, so relative humidity falls; at night cooling raises relative humidity, possibly to 100% (dew or fog).

items.stem: Explain the weather associated with stable air.
items.answer: Rising air is suppressed: few clouds or layered stratus, little precipitation, possible fog and inversions, pollution trapped.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point [3]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “Unstable air often produces towering cumulus clouds and showers.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain conditional instability.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Air keeps rising and cooling, condensing to form deep convective cloud. (b) The ELR lies between the SALR and DALR; unsaturated rising air cools at the DALR and is cooler than its surroundings (stable); once condensation occurs it cools at the slower SALR and may become warmer than the surroundings, so it continues to rise (unstable).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark definition; 1 mark below condensation; 1 mark above [3]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the growth of ice crystals at the expense of supercooled water droplets in clouds below 0 °C, producing precipitation”.
items.answer: Bergeron-Findeisen process
items.markingKey: Bergeron-Findeisen process: the growth of ice crystals at the expense of supercooled water droplets in clouds below 0 °C, producing precipitation. [1]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the growth of raindrops in warm clouds as droplets collide and merge”.
items.answer: Collision-coalescence
items.markingKey: Collision-coalescence: the growth of raindrops in warm clouds as droplets collide and merge. [1]

items.stem: Explain the Bergeron-Findeisen process of precipitation formation.
items.answer: In clouds between about 0 and −40 °C, ice crystals and supercooled droplets coexist; saturation vapour pressure is lower over ice, so vapour deposits on ice crystals, which grow at the expense of droplets, become heavy and fall, melting to rain if the air below is warm.
items.markingKey: 1 mark coexistence; 1 mark vapour pressure; 1 mark growth and fall [3]

items.stem: Table 6.2 shows mean annual precipitation (mm) along a transect across the Western Ghats, India, in the direction of the prevailing wind: windward coast (0 m) 1 376, windward slope (800 m) 2 807, summit (1500 m) 3 403, leeward slope (800 m) 672, leeward lowland (100 m) 395. Explain why the leeward side is much drier.
items.answer: Air has lost much moisture on the windward side; descending air warms adiabatically at the DALR, so relative humidity falls and clouds evaporate (rain shadow).
items.markingKey: 1 mark moisture lost; 1 mark descending warming [2]

items.stem: Outline the evidence that supports, and the evidence that challenges, the view that the type of uplift is more important than temperature in determining the form of precipitation.
items.answer: For: Strong convective uplift creates cumulonimbus with hail; gentle frontal uplift gives steady rain or drizzle; orographic uplift gives persistent rain. Against: Temperature decides whether precipitation falls as rain, snow, sleet or hail; ice-crystal processes need sub-zero cloud tops; dew and rime depend on surface temperature. Conclusion: Uplift controls the intensity and type of cloud, but temperature through the cloud and below it decides the form that reaches the ground.

items.stem: Explain the formation of hail.
items.answer: In tall cumulonimbus clouds strong updraughts carry ice pellets repeatedly through layers of supercooled water, adding layers of ice until they are too heavy to be held up.
items.markingKey: 1 mark updraughts; 1 mark layers; 1 mark fall [3]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the natural warming of the Earth’s surface by gases that absorb and re-emit long-wave radiation”.
items.answer: Greenhouse effect
items.markingKey: Greenhouse effect: the natural warming of the Earth’s surface by gases that absorb and re-emit long-wave radiation. [1]

items.stem: Explain how the enhanced greenhouse effect leads to global warming.
items.answer: Burning fossil fuels, deforestation and agriculture increase concentrations of CO₂, methane and nitrous oxide; these absorb more outgoing long-wave radiation and re-emit it towards the surface, raising mean temperatures.
items.markingKey: 1 mark sources; 1 mark absorption; 1 mark re-emission/warming [3]

items.stem: Explain two possible impacts of global warming on people.
items.answer: Sea-level rise threatening coastal cities and deltas (Bangladesh, Maldives); more intense droughts, heatwaves and floods; changing crop yields; spread of diseases such as malaria; loss of glaciers that supply water.
items.markingKey: 1 mark impact; 1 mark development each [4]

items.stem: “The effects of global warming will be felt most severely by people in low-income countries.” Discuss.
items.answer: For: LICs depend on rain-fed farming; low-lying deltas (Bangladesh) and small islands (Tuvalu, Maldives) face sea-level rise; less money for adaptation; heat stress; health systems weak. Against: HICs also face wildfires (Australia, California), heatwaves (Europe 2003, 2022) and coastal flooding; some high-latitude areas may benefit from longer growing seasons; vulnerability varies within countries. Conclusion: Impacts are global, but poverty, dependence on agriculture and limited adaptive capacity mean the poorest people are most severely affected.

At Manila at midday the air temperature is 30 °C and the absolute humidity is 25.5 g/m³. (a) Explain what would happen to the relative humidity if the air cooled overnight without any change in its moisture content. (b) Suggest why relative humidity is often higher in the early morning than in the afternoon.
items.answer: (a) Relative humidity would rise because cooler air can hold less vapour; at the dew point it reaches 100% and dew, fog or frost may form. (b) Temperatures are lowest at dawn, so saturation vapour content is lowest and RH highest.

items.stem: Air at sea level with a temperature of 28 °C and a dew point of 17 °C is forced to rise over a mountain range 2 500 m high, then descends to sea level on the other side. Assume a DALR of 10 °C per 1000 m, a SALR of 5 °C per 1000 m, that condensation begins when the air has cooled to 17 °C, and that all moisture is lost as precipitation on the windward side. (a) Calculate the temperature of the air when it reaches sea level on the leeward side. (b) Explain why the air is warmer on the leeward side than at the same height on the windward side.
items.answer: (a) 35 °C (b) On the windward side, above the condensation level, air cooled at the slower SALR because latent heat was released; descending air warms at the faster DALR; this is the föhn effect.
items.markingKey: (a) descends dry at the DALR: 10 + 10 × 2.5 = 35 °C [2] (b) 1 mark SALR/latent heat; 1 mark DALR descent; 1 mark föhn [3]

items.stem: Explain why condensation nuclei are needed for clouds to form.
items.answer: Pure air would need to be supersaturated for droplets to form; nuclei provide surfaces for vapour to condense onto at about 100% relative humidity.

items.stem: “The type of uplift is more important than temperature in determining the form of precipitation.” How far do you agree with this statement? In your answer you may refer to convection and freezing level.
items.answer: For: Strong convective uplift creates cumulonimbus with hail; gentle frontal uplift gives steady rain or drizzle; orographic uplift gives persistent rain. Against: Temperature decides whether precipitation falls as rain, snow, sleet or hail; ice-crystal processes need sub-zero cloud tops; dew and rime depend on surface temperature. Conclusion: Uplift controls the intensity and type of cloud, but temperature through the cloud and below it decides the form that reaches the ground.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “greenhouse effect”?
options: The natural warming of the Earth’s surface by gases that absorb and re-emit long-wave radiation.
The increase in the greenhouse effect caused by human emissions of greenhouse gases, leading to global warming.
A gas such as carbon dioxide, methane or nitrous oxide that absorbs long-wave radiation.
A store that absorbs more carbon than it releases, such as forests, soils and oceans.
items.answer: The natural warming of the Earth’s surface by gases that absorb and re-emit long-wave radiation.
items.markingKey: Greenhouse effect: the natural warming of the Earth’s surface by gases that absorb and re-emit long-wave radiation. [1]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Global warming may cause some places to become colder or wetter.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Changes in circulation and ocean currents produce regional variations, not uniform warming.

items.stem: A revision website states: “Deforestation contributes to the enhanced greenhouse effect.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Burning and decay release stored carbon and remove a carbon sink.

items.stem: Fig. 6.3 shows the annual mean concentration of carbon dioxide at Mauna Loa, Hawaii (ppm): 1960: 316.9, 1970: 325.7, 1980: 338.8, 1990: 354.4, 2000: 369.7, 2010: 389.9, 2020: 414.2, 2023: 421.1. The pre-industrial concentration was about 280 ppm. Explain why a seasonal rise and fall is seen within each year at Mauna Loa.
items.answer: Northern Hemisphere vegetation absorbs CO₂ by photosynthesis in summer and releases it by decay in winter.

items.stem: Air at sea level with a temperature of 27 °C and a dew point of 15 °C is forced to rise over a mountain range 3 000 m high, then descends to sea level on the other side. On another day the ELR is 6.5 °C per 1000 m. State the stability of the atmosphere and give a reason.
items.answer: Conditionally unstable: the ELR is between the SALR and DALR, so air becomes unstable only after condensation.

items.stem: Assess the view that the effects of global warming will be felt most severely by people in low-income countries.
items.answer: For: LICs depend on rain-fed farming; low-lying deltas (Bangladesh) and small islands (Tuvalu, Maldives) face sea-level rise; less money for adaptation; heat stress; health systems weak. Against: HICs also face wildfires (Australia, California), heatwaves (Europe 2003, 2022) and coastal flooding; some high-latitude areas may benefit from longer growing seasons; vulnerability varies within countries. Conclusion: Impacts are global, but poverty, dependence on agriculture and limited adaptive capacity mean the poorest people are most severely affected.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain the weather associated with stable air. (b) A student writes: “The DALR changes from day to day.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Rising air is suppressed: few clouds or layered stratus, little precipitation, possible fog and inversions, pollution trapped. (b) Not correct. The DALR is fixed (about 10 °C/km); it is the ELR that varies.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per point [3] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain conditional instability. (b) A revision website states: “Relative humidity can be 100% without rain falling.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) The ELR lies between the SALR and DALR; unsaturated rising air cools at the DALR and is cooler than its surroundings (stable); once condensation occurs it cools at the slower SALR and may become warmer than the surroundings, so it continues to rise (unstable). (b) Correct. Saturated air may produce fog or cloud but droplets must grow large enough to fall.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “enhanced greenhouse effect”?
options: A store that absorbs more carbon than it releases, such as forests, soils and oceans.
A process that amplifies an initial change, for example melting ice lowering albedo and causing more warming.
The increase in the greenhouse effect caused by human emissions of greenhouse gases, leading to global warming.
A gas such as carbon dioxide, methane or nitrous oxide that absorbs long-wave radiation.
items.answer: The increase in the greenhouse effect caused by human emissions of greenhouse gases, leading to global warming.
items.markingKey: Enhanced greenhouse effect: the increase in the greenhouse effect caused by human emissions of greenhouse gases, leading to global warming. [1]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why it is difficult to predict future global temperatures. (b) A student writes: “The greenhouse effect is entirely caused by human activity.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Uncertain future emissions (economic growth, policies); complex feedbacks (clouds, ice, permafrost); natural variability (El Niño, volcanoes); limitations of climate models. (b) Not correct. The natural greenhouse effect keeps the Earth about 33 °C warmer than it would be; humans have enhanced it.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain how the enhanced greenhouse effect leads to global warming. (b) A student writes: “The greenhouse effect is entirely caused by human activity.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Burning fossil fuels, deforestation and agriculture increase concentrations of CO₂, methane and nitrous oxide; these absorb more outgoing long-wave radiation and re-emit it towards the surface, raising mean temperatures. (b) Not correct. The natural greenhouse effect keeps the Earth about 33 °C warmer than it would be; humans have enhanced it.
